summary.text: Sea level rise is the climb in the world's average sea level, which rose 15–25 cm between 1901 and 2018 and is now speeding up.
Human-caused climate change is the main driver, through melting ice sheets and glaciers plus water expanding as it warms.
Because the sea responds to warming decades late, it will keep accelerating to 2050, and later rise depends on future emissions.

facts.label: Exposed countries
facts.value: Twelve of the top twenty countries are in Asia

items.prompt: No ice melts at all, yet the ocean keeps getting warmer. Would sea level still rise?

options.label: No, only melting ice can add to the sea
Yes, because warmer water takes up more room
No, warm water evaporates and the sea drops
Yes, because warm water pulls in more rain

items.explain: Thermal expansion of warming water caused about 42% of sea level rise between 1993 and 2018.

items.prompt: Suppose the world stopped all extra warming today. What would sea level do over the next couple of decades?

options.label: Start falling right away
Stop rising almost at once
Keep rising and speeding up until about 2050
Rise only during stormy years

items.explain: Sea level lags temperature by decades, so warming that has already happened keeps it accelerating until 2050.

items.prompt: A coastal city's sea level is climbing two to three times faster than the global figure. What best explains a local difference like this?

options.label: The global average is measured wrongly
Ocean water piles up near big cities
The city is closer to melting glaciers
Local factors such as the land itself sinking

items.explain: Local factors like tidal range and land subsidence strongly change impacts; some land is sinking while other land rises.

items.prompt: A farming village near the coast sees its harvests shrink as the sea rises, even though its fields never flood. What is a likely cause?

options.label: Saltier water reaching the irrigation supply
Cooler air drifting in from the sea
Less sunlight from more frequent fog
Fewer bees because of rising tides

items.explain: Rising salt levels in irrigation water can reduce crop yields, one knock-on effect of higher seas.

items.prompt: A beach town decides to pump sand onto its eroding shore and restore its dunes instead of building a seawall. What kind of adaptation is this?

options.label: A hard approach
A soft approach
Managed retreat
Emissions cutting

items.explain: Dune rehabilitation and beach nourishment are soft approaches, while seawalls are hard ones.

items.prompt: In the near term, which places will feel the biggest impact of rising seas on people?

options.label: Mountain towns beside large lakes
Inland cities along major rivers
Coastal cities in cold northern countries
Low-lying Caribbean and Pacific islands

items.explain: Low-lying Caribbean and Pacific islands, including atolls, face the greatest near-term impact, and many may become uninhabitable this century.
